page_lead: Information for pregnant women and partners to review with safety and reassurance in mind.
intro_title: Sex During Pregnancy: For Pregnant Women and Their Partners
intro_copy: Review whether sex is possible, when to avoid it, body changes, positions, and safety points by theme.
intro_note: Illustrations: Created with ChatGPT / Supervised by an obstetrician-gynecologist
item_1_detail: If the pregnancy is progressing normally, sex is generally possible when a condom is used and the abdomen is not put under pressure. Sex itself does not often directly cause miscarriage or preterm birth. However, depending on the mother’s condition or the baby’s condition, it may be better to avoid sex. It is not “safe for everyone at all times,” so consult a doctor or midwife if you have any concerns.
item_2_detail: Avoid sex and consult medical staff if you have abdominal tightening or lower abdominal pain, have been told you have threatened miscarriage or threatened preterm labor, have genital bleeding, have bleeding or a hematoma in early pregnancy, have placenta previa or a low-lying placenta, have rupture of membranes or suspected rupture, have cervical insufficiency, have a high-risk multiple pregnancy, or have been instructed by a doctor to rest.
item_3_title: 3. Changes in the body and emotions during pregnancy
item_3_detail: During pregnancy, the body and emotions change greatly, so the way sex feels may also change. The uterus is made of muscle and may tighten lightly. Components in semen or nipple stimulation can make the uterus contract more easily. The vagina and vulva may become more sensitive because blood flow increases, and discharge may increase. Nipple stimulation can release oxytocin and cause abdominal tightening. Sexual desire may become stronger or weaker, or you may not want to be touched. Any of these feelings can be natural.
item_4_title: 4. Points to be careful about during pregnancy
item_4_detail: Choose positions that do not press on the abdomen. Side-lying positions, positions supported from behind, or positions where the pregnant person can control movement and depth may reduce strain. Avoid positions where the partner’s weight presses on the abdomen, especially lying flat on the back after mid-pregnancy. Do not force yourself when tired, in pain, anxious, or not in the mood. Use condoms to help prevent infection and reduce semen-related uterine contractions. Contact the hospital after sex if you have bleeding, strong abdominal pain, regular tightening, or watery fluid that may be rupture of membranes.
item_5_detail: In early pregnancy, miscarriage is more common and nausea or poor condition may occur, so do not overdo it. Avoid sex if there is bleeding or abdominal pain. In mid-pregnancy the condition is often more stable, but the abdomen begins to grow, so avoiding pressure is important. In late pregnancy the abdomen is larger and may tighten more easily. Especially after 36 weeks, be cautious because sex may be connected with rupture of membranes, infection, or labor.
item_6_detail: Use a condom. Avoid vigorous movement. Avoid strong nipple stimulation. Do not press on the abdomen. Do not force yourself.
item_7_detail: The most important points are not putting strain on the abdomen, feeling safe, and not forcing yourself. If you feel even a little pain or anxiety, it is okay to stop. Sex is not only sexual intercourse; it is also one form of important communication with a partner. During pregnancy, physical condition and feelings can change easily, so sex is not necessary if it feels difficult. Holding hands, hugging, and spending time together can also be reassuring forms of closeness. Share your feelings with each other and put the pregnant person’s condition first.
